newsitem.title: FRANCE: French groups seek to extend law to cyberspace.
newsitem.headline: French groups seek to extend law to cyberspace.

text.p: Defenders of the French language urged a Paris court on Monday to extend France's laws into cyberspace by banning the French campus of an American university from using only English on an Internet site.
The court heard a legal challenge by two private French groups against a site on the global computer network that was set up by the French campus of the Georgia Institute of Technology.
Georgia Tech Lorraine, based in the eastern French city of Metz, argued that communications on the Internet were like telephone calls and outside legislation promoting French culture and language.

Since 1994 legislation known as the Toubon law has required that all advertising in France be in French, part of a long-running battle to protect the language of Moliere and Racine against the growing global grip of English.
An advertisement can feature other languages as well, but only if they are translated into French.

"Users of the Internet must respect French law. We consider that French citizens have a right to the respect of their language," Marc Jobert, lawyer for the two groups, Defence of the French Language and Future of the French Language, told Reuters.
They urged the court to force Georgia Tech Lorraine to pay a fine and damages of 20,000 francs ($4,000) and oblige it to translate the Internet site into French.
Lawyers for Georgia Tech Lorraine said the site was in English because all its courses were taught in English and all its students were required to be fluent English-speakers.
"We're not opposed to the use of French on the site but we don't have to do it," said Jacques Schaefer, lawyer for Georgia Tech in Metz.
He said the information posted in cyberspace by the university was "private messages, in which legislators should not meddle, just like the telephone".
Schaefer added: "The fact that the exchange is made via a screen makes it no different from a telephone conversation. The Toubon law is a law with only a restricted application."
The court said it would issue a ruling on the case, likely to have wide implications for the reach of national laws over the Internet, on February 24.

The Georgia Tech Lorraine site -- whose Internet address is www.georgiatech-metz.fr -- offers course descriptions, a guide to the campus and other information for current and potential students. Most of the students at the campus are French.
The site also provides access to Internet pages put together by some students.
Georgia Tech Lorraine says it has received a flood of electronic messages backing its stand, with only a tiny number against.

Mickey Mouse became the first victim of the Toubon law in March 1995 when a Paris court condemned a Disney store in Paris for failing to label about 10 types of toys with safety advice in French alongside the English stickers.
Foreign companies say the legislation is a disincentive to holding conferences in France. The law requires French translation of any meeting held in English.
